changes.before:
Accountability in public service means being answerable, not being blamed. When you hold a public role, your work reaches people who did not choose you and often cannot go elsewhere. A person receiving services, a family member, a county partner and a coworker each have a fair claim to an explanation of what you did and why. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide, written for state employees, describes state leaders as accountable to all Minnesotans and expects leaders to take accountability for their own actions. Blame looks back for someone to punish. Answerability looks at what happened, who it affected and what happens next.

Most public servants answer to several groups at once. You answer to the people served, whose lives the work touches. You answer to colleagues who rely on your part being done well. You answer to the public, whose trust and money fund the work. You answer to the law and to agency policy. Some of these duties are set in law. Minnesota's code of ethics for executive branch employees, section 43A.38 of Minnesota Statutes, says that when an employee believes a conflict of interest may exist, it is the employee's duty to avoid the situation. Other habits in this course, such as asking for correction or reporting back, are good practice you choose. Keep the two apart.

A short map shows who a decision reaches. First, name the decision or piece of work. Second, list who it reaches: the people served, partners, coworkers, the public and any rule that applies. Third, ask whose experience you have not heard and how you would find out. Fourth, ask who decides each part and what evidence you have. Many of us learned at work that being accountable means answering to the person above us. That is a real duty. But a habit that only checks upward can miss the people a decision lands on, often the people with the least say in it.

Being answerable does not mean you decide everything or carry every outcome alone. You can explain your own choices, invite questions and fix what is yours to fix. Formal judgments about conduct, discipline and complaints belong to Human Resources, labor relations or the equal opportunity office. Under section 43A.38, a possible conflict of interest is yours to avoid and can be determined by you, your appointing authority or the commissioner, so raise it promptly. Answerability is the daily practice underneath those processes. It is not a substitute for them.

changes.before:
An open door is not the same as an easy door. Telling a leader they are wrong carries risk, and the risk is larger for people with less power: a newer employee, someone in a temporary role, a provider whose license you review or a person whose services depend on your decision. A perspective published by the federal Patient Safety Network describes team psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, and names hierarchy and authoritarian leadership among the barriers. Silence may say more about the cost of speaking than about the quality of your work.

Leaders can lower the cost of speaking up, though the evidence has limits. In Deloitte research on inclusive leadership, Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke describe humility as admitting mistakes, acknowledging limits and seeking others' input. A 2026 umbrella review by Gonzalez and colleagues found listening, transparency and sharing power among the leader behaviors linked to psychological safety, and the authors suggest that leaders model vulnerability, for example by admitting mistakes. Most of this research comes from health care and general management studies, not public human services. The reviewers note that the usual definition reflects a Western, individualist view and that culture, race and ethnicity are little examined, and they call for research that also looks at disability. The practical point still holds: people watch what happens to the first person who disagrees.

Inviting correction looks different at different points on IDI, LLC's Intercultural Development Continuum. A Minimization habit sounds fair: my door is open to everyone, so anyone can tell me. An Acceptance habit notices that people learned different rules about whether and how to disagree with someone above them, and that your own rule is only one of them. An Adaptation habit changes the method. You ask a specific question, such as which step in this checklist does not work. You offer a written route and a later one-to-one. You go first by naming something you may have missed, and report what you changed. These describe habits, not people. Nobody should guess or label a colleague's orientation.

Asking for correction is the easier half of the work. Trust grows when you act on what you hear and say what you did, including when you decide not to change something and why. Do not press anyone to name who said what. If what you hear is about harassment, discrimination or a possible accommodation, it is no longer only feedback. It goes to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office.

changes.before:
Owning a mistake starts with what happened to the other person, not with your reasons. When public servants get something wrong, the effect often lands on someone with little power to push back: a family that missed a deadline, a provider that changed staffing or a coworker who redid work. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide lists admitting that you are not always right among the expert behaviors for leading yourself. It is a skill you can practice, and a plain structure makes it easier.

A clear ownership statement names what you did, its effect on the other person and what you are doing now. In plain words: I sent the letter with the wrong due date. Say the effect as the other person experienced it, and ask about what you do not know: you moved staff and changed people's schedules to meet a date that was not real, so what else did it cost you? Then say what you are doing now and when. Keep your reasons short and put them after the effect. An explanation that helps the person know what to expect is useful. An explanation that shifts the weight onto the template, the system or the workload is defending, even when it is true.

Repair puts right the effect on the person, changes the step that let the mistake through and reports back. First, put right what you can for the person who was affected, and check with them whether it actually helps. Second, find the step that let the mistake through and change it, so the next person is not affected. Third, tell the people who were affected what you changed. Many of us learned to fix errors quietly and move on, because it feels less awkward. A quiet fix corrects the record but leaves the person wondering whether it will happen again, and whether anyone noticed what it cost them.

Part of owning a mistake is knowing which parts of the repair are yours. You can acknowledge the mistake, correct your own work and change your own practice. You should not promise outcomes you do not control, such as waiving a requirement, changing a licensing decision or offering compensation. Those belong to your supervisor and the responsible program area, and legal questions belong to legal counsel. If the mistake may have exposed private data, or may involve discrimination or harassment, tell your supervisor promptly so the right process can start.

changes.before:
Trust grows when people can see what happened to what you said you would do. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide connects building trust with following through on commitments and communicating openly. Most broken commitments are not broken on purpose. They fade: a promise made in a meeting, a busy month, then silence. To the people who were waiting, silence reads as an answer.

Closing the loop means telling people where a commitment stands, even when the news is not good. A useful update says what you said you would do, what you have done, what is still open, what you decided not to do and why, and when you will next report. If the answer is no, say so and give the reason. People can plan around a clear no far better than around silence, and a clear no is still a way of answering to them. Keep commitments where the people affected can see them, such as a short list you review at each team meeting. Track the work, not the people. The list records what was promised and where it stands, and it never holds notes about individual staff.

Some matters that surface while you follow through belong to a formal process. A possible accommodation request goes to Human Resources, a concern about harassment, discrimination or retaliation goes to Human Resources and the equal opportunity office, and a labor agreement question goes to labor relations. When a commitment turns into a formal matter, your promise changes shape. You can no longer promise the result, but you can still promise to move it today, to tell people where it went and to report on the parts that stay yours. Talk with the person privately, not in front of the team. Promising a result or settling it yourself can skip protections that exist for that person.

Handing a matter on is not the same as dropping it. You stay answerable for the parts that remain yours: telling people where the matter went, in general terms that protect privacy, keeping the rest of the commitment moving and checking back when you said you would. For any commitment, ask the closing question: what happened, for whom, and what will I keep, change or stop? Then give that answer to the people who were waiting.

changes.before:
An open door is not the same as an easy door. Telling a leader they are wrong carries risk, and the risk is larger for people with less power: a newer employee, someone in a temporary role, a provider whose license you review or a person whose services depend on your decision. A perspective published by the federal Patient Safety Network describes team psychological safety as a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, and names hierarchy and authoritarian leadership among the barriers. Silence alone does not establish either the quality of the work or why someone has not raised a concern.

Leaders can lower the cost of speaking up, though the evidence has limits. In Deloitte research on inclusive leadership, Bernadette Dillon and Juliet Bourke describe humility as admitting mistakes, acknowledging limits and seeking others' input. A 2026 umbrella review by Gonzalez and colleagues found listening, transparency and sharing power among the leader behaviors linked to psychological safety, and the authors suggest that leaders model vulnerability, for example by admitting mistakes. Most of this research comes from health care and general management studies, not public human services. The reviewers note that the usual definition reflects a Western, individualist view and that culture, race and ethnicity are little examined, and they call for research that also looks at disability. Consider how your response to disagreement may affect someone’s willingness to raise a later concern.

The following program examples use vocabulary from IDI, LLC’s Intercultural Development Continuum to compare approaches to correction. They are illustrations, not a way to determine anyone’s orientation. A Minimization habit sounds fair: my door is open to everyone, so anyone can tell me. An Acceptance habit notices that people learned different rules about whether and how to disagree with someone above them, and that your own rule is only one of them. An Adaptation habit changes the method. You ask a specific question, such as which step in this checklist does not work. You offer a written route and a later one-to-one. You go first by naming something you may have missed, and report what you changed. These describe habits, not people. Nobody should guess or label a colleague's orientation.

Asking for correction is the easier half of the work. Explain what you changed after hearing feedback and, when you leave something unchanged, give the reason. Do not pressure someone to identify coworkers merely to establish who disagrees with you. An authorized complaint process may need relevant facts, so explain any reporting duties and confidentiality limits. Route possible harassment, discrimination or accommodation concerns through the applicable agency process rather than treating them only as suggestions.

Accountability in public service means being answerable, not being blamed. When you hold a public role, your work reaches people who did not choose you and often cannot go elsewhere. People receiving services, family members, partners and coworkers may need an explanation of decisions that affect them. Give relevant information through an appropriate channel while protecting private records and respecting each person’s authority to receive it. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency guide, written for state employees, describes state leaders as accountable to all Minnesotans and expects leaders to take accountability for their own actions. Blame looks back for someone to punish. Answerability looks at what happened, who it affected and what happens next.

Most public servants answer to several groups at once. You answer to the people served, whose lives the work touches. You answer to colleagues who rely on your part being done well. You answer to the public, whose trust and money fund the work. You answer to the law and to agency policy. Some of these duties are set in law.
